# 2 Maccabees Chapter 5 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 5 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_005_page_001.jpg

---

**1** Around this time Antiochus launched his second campaign against Egypt.

**2** For nearly forty days the people of Jerusalem witnessed something extraordinary: troops appeared in the sky above the city — cavalry riding in gold armor, whole units in battle formation, spears and swords at the ready —

**3** squadrons forming up, charges and countercharges, shields clashing, spear-lines advancing, arrows in flight, golden ornaments gleaming, armor of every kind.

**4** Everyone prayed that this vision would turn out to be a good sign.

**5** Then a false rumor spread that Antiochus had died. Jason seized the moment — he gathered over a thousand men and launched a sudden assault on the city. The defenders on the wall were pushed back, the city was falling into his hands, and Menelaus had to flee to the citadel.

**6** Jason went on killing his own people without the slightest mercy. He didn't understand that when you triumph over your own countrymen, there is no victory — only disaster. He thought he was raising victory monuments over enemies. They were his own people.

**7** In the end he gained nothing. His plot earned him nothing but humiliation, and he was forced to flee yet again into Ammonite territory.

**8** His end was wretched. Aretas, king of the Arabs, had him arrested. He fled from city to city, hunted down by everyone. All nations despised him — the man who had betrayed his country's laws and slaughtered his own people. He washed up on the shore of Egypt,

**9** and there the man who had sent so many of his countrymen into exile died in exile himself — after trying to sail to Sparta in the hope that the Spartans, claiming kinship with the Jews, might offer him refuge.

**10** He had left countless others to lie unburied. Now he lay unburied himself. There was no one to mourn him, no funeral, no place in his ancestors' tomb.

**11** When word of what had happened reached Antiochus, he took it as a sign of rebellion. Furious, he marched out of Egypt and fell upon Jerusalem with the full force of his army.

**12** He ordered his soldiers to show no mercy — to cut down everyone they encountered and to slaughter those who had taken shelter in their homes.

**13** Young men and old men were butchered together. Women and children were slaughtered. Virgins and infants were put to the sword.

**14** In three days, eighty thousand people were killed — forty thousand in direct combat, and as many more were sold into slavery.

**15** Even that was not enough for him. He had the gall to enter the most holy temple on earth, led by Menelaus — the man who had betrayed both the law and his own country.

**16** His defiled hands grabbed the sacred vessels. His profane hands swept away gifts that other kings had given to enhance and glorify and honor the place.

**17** Antiochus was drunk with his own importance. He could not see what was really happening: that the LORD had allowed this, for a brief time, as a judgment on the sins of the people who lived in the city. That was why the holy place had been left unprotected.

**18** Had they not been so deeply sunk in sin, Antiochus would have been beaten back the moment he set foot in the city — driven away in humiliation, just as Heliodorus had been when Seleucus sent him to loot the treasury.

**19** But God had not chosen the nation for the sake of the holy place. He had chosen the holy place for the sake of the nation.

**20** That is why the sanctuary shared in the suffering of the nation — and would share in its restoration. The place that was abandoned in the hour of God's anger would be fully restored when the great LORD had been appeased.

**21** Antiochus stripped the temple of eighteen hundred talents and hurried back to Antioch. In his delusion, he actually thought himself powerful enough to make the sea walkable and the land navigable. That is how inflated his mind had become.

**22** He left officials behind to crush the people: Philip, a Phrygian, was installed at Jerusalem — a man even more barbarous than the king who appointed him.

**23** At Gerizim he left Andronicus, and alongside these he left Menelaus himself, who oppressed the Jewish citizens more brutally than all the rest. In his vicious hatred of his own people,

**24** Antiochus sent a general named Apollonius — commander of the Mysian mercenaries — with twenty-two thousand troops. His orders: kill every adult male; sell the women and the young.

**25** Apollonius arrived in Jerusalem and played the peacemaker. He waited. When the sabbath came and the Jews were at rest, he had his soldiers march out in full battle gear —

**26** and everyone who came out to watch was cut down. Then he charged the city with his entire force and killed enormous numbers.

**27** But Judas Maccabeus, with about nine companions, escaped into the wilderness. They lived in the mountains like wild animals, surviving on whatever plants they could find, because they would not set foot in the defiled city.
